title: Sepsis: recognising it and the first hour

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.a: Infection with organ dysfunction, a SOFA rise of 2 or more
d: Two SIRS criteria with a positive culture
questions.why: Septic shock adds the need for vasopressors to keep a mean pressure of 65 and a lactate over 2 despite fluids. SIRS still has a role in screening, but not in the definition.

questions.q: What does the guideline say about using qSOFA alone to screen for sepsis?
questions.a: Not recommended as a single screening tool; it is too insensitive
d: It should be used only in intensive care
questions.why: Early warning scores such as NEWS or MEWS, or SIRS, catch more patients earlier. qSOFA positivity marks a patient who is already very sick.

questions.q: In septic shock, within how long of recognition should antibiotics be given?
questions.why: Also within an hour for probable sepsis without shock. If sepsis is possible but unconfirmed and there is no shock, there is a three-hour window to investigate before committing.

questions.q: Blood cultures have not yet been drawn and antibiotics are due. What happens?
questions.a: Draw cultures now and give antibiotics at once; neither waits long for the other
d: Delay antibiotics until cultures are back
Give a single dose and wait for cultures before the second
questions.why: Cultures before antibiotics are ideal, but each hour of delay in shock raises mortality. Sputum, urine and site cultures follow.

questions.q: For sepsis-induced hypotension or a lactate of 4 or more, how much crystalloid is given in the first three hours?
questions.why: Balanced crystalloids are preferred over saline. Further fluid is guided by dynamic measures of responsiveness rather than a fixed target.

questions.q: Which vasopressor is first line in septic shock?
questions.why: Vasopressin is added when the norepinephrine dose reaches about 0.25 to 0.5 micrograms per kg per minute. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias.

questions.q: What mean arterial pressure is targeted in septic shock?
questions.why: Higher targets did not improve survival and increased atrial fibrillation. Vasopressors can be started through a good peripheral line while central access is arranged.

questions.q: A lactate is 3.5 on arrival. When is it remeasured?
questions.why: Lactate clearance guides resuscitation. A lactate that fails to fall means the source, the fluids, or the pressor plan needs rethinking.

questions.q: When is hydrocortisone given in septic shock?
questions.a: When vasopressor need persists, about norepinephrine 0.25 micrograms per kg per minute or more
questions.why: The dose is 200 mg a day. It shortens shock and time on pressors; the effect on mortality is small.

questions.q: Within how long should source control, such as draining an abscess or removing an infected line, be achieved?
questions.why: Antibiotics cannot sterilise an undrained collection. The hunt for a source that needs a procedure starts at the same time as the antibiotics.

questions.q: Cultures return with a sensitive organism after 48 hours of broad antibiotics. What happens?
questions.a: Narrow the antibiotics to target it
d: Continue the broad regimen for the full course
questions.why: Daily reassessment for de-escalation is part of the bundle. Procalcitonin can support a decision to stop, and shorter courses are preferred when the source is controlled.

questions.q: Above what glucose is an insulin infusion started in a septic patient in intensive care?
questions.why: Two readings above 180 trigger an insulin infusion aimed at 144 to 180. Tighter control caused hypoglycaemia and more deaths in the intensive care trials.
